sources.title: UNESCO: Dacian Fortresses of the Orastie Mountains
sources.note: Brief synthesis and criteria: six defensive works, religious and military architecture, first century BCE to first century CE. Does not validate imported borders.

sources.title: ICOMOS: Dacian Fortresses evaluation, 1999
sources.note: Dacia evaluation, PDF pages 143 to 146: Burebista, terraces, sanctuaries, workshops, water and 106 conquest. Avoids erroneous statements elsewhere about Herodotus and the location of the later Roman capital.

sources.title: Beatrice Ciuta: Archaeobotanical investigations on samples recovered from Dacian settlements located in Transylvanian area, 2023
sources.note: Accessible abstract only: charred plant remains from seven Transylvanian sites, cereals, legumes and fruits. Full article download was inaccessible.

sources.title: Beatrice Ciuta: Plants, Power, and Connectivity, conference abstract, 2025
sources.note: Printed pages 22 to 23, PDF pages 22 to 23: wheat, barley, rye, millet, pulses, flax and camelina; storage and textile interpretation. Conference abstract, not a full published excavation report.

sources.title: CIMEC: Excavations in the Orastie Mountains, 1949 to 1959
sources.note: Indexed institutional excavation history, 1954 account: furnace workshop, iron tools, painted pottery, glass and stamped vessel. Direct retrieval failed with an encoding error; indexed text was read.

sources.title: Technical University of Cluj-Napoca: DACIT heritage project
sources.note: Project description: Mediterranean commercial exchange, iron metallurgy, fortresses and three-dimensional documentation of everyday objects.

sources.title: Dumitru Protase: Decebalus per Scorilo, a new interpretation, 1986
sources.note: Thraco-Dacica VII, pages 146 to 153. Opening description and pages 152 to 153 discuss stamps, competing interpretations and the author’s proposed Latin reading. This interpretation is not presented as scholarly consensus.

sources.title: Gica Baestean: Ceramic water pipes in Colonia Dacica Sarmizegetusa, 1997 to 1998
sources.note: Sargetia XXVII/1, pages 253 to 260: 22 ceramic pipe sections at the procurator’s palace; suggested bath supply around 170; loose tubes also used in vault construction. This concerns Roman Ulpia Traiana Sarmizegetusa, not the mountain capital.

sources.title: Imola Boda: The Sacred Topography of Colonia Sarmizegetusa, 2015
sources.note: Acta Antiqua 55, pages 281 to 304, especially page 287: two Severan nymphaea beside the Trajanic forum, water supply and dedication by L. Ophonius Domitius Priscus.

sources.title: UNESCO: Frontiers of the Roman Empire, Dacia
sources.note: Property synthesis: Roman province and frontier from 106 to 271 CE, military and civilian settlements, extraction and exchange. Unrelated introductory dating claim is not used.

proposedOverrides.summary: Dacian communities preceded the Roman province of Dacia. This shared card distinguishes everyday archaeological evidence, pre-Roman kingdoms and later Roman urban life; it does not treat a people as one unchanging state.

batchIdentityNotes.assessment: Imported Dacia state coverage approximately 1 BCE to 200 CE spans both pre-Roman kingdom and Roman provincial history. Decoded BCE1 and CE100 outlines span approximately 21.735 to 27.340 E, 43.821 to 47.700 N. Narrative explicitly distinguishes conquest in 106, Roman provincial period and map endpoint. No successor geometry certified.

Imported cultural record approximately 100 to 1 BCE, decoded BCE100 polygon spans 21.706 to 29.083 E, 40.915 to 47.127 N, with an overbroad southern reach toward the Aegean. Shared narrative covers overlapping people and their later political history; this does not equate cultural, royal and provincial borders. Public overview labels outlines broad approximations. No extinction or unified boundary inferred.
